claim: CUT&RUN is a chromatin profiling strategy in which antibody-targeted controlled cleavage by micrococcal nuclease releases specific protein-DNA complexes into the supernatant for paired-end DNA sequencing.
source: We describe Cleavage Under Targets and Release Using Nuclease (CUT&RUN), a chromatin profiling strategy in which antibody-targeted controlled cleavage by micrococcal nuclease releases specific protein-DNA complexes into the supernatant for paired-end DNA sequencing.
evidence: This is the primary description of the CUT&RUN method presented in the abstract, supported by the entire manuscript's experimental data and methodology.

claim: Unlike ChIP, which fragments and solubilizes total chromatin, CUT&RUN is performed in situ.
source: Unlike Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP), which fragments and solubilizes total chromatin, CUT&RUN is performed in situ, allowing for both quantitative high-resolution chromatin mapping and probing of the local chromatin environment.
evidence: This is a direct comparison between CUT&RUN and ChIP methodologies, supported by the experimental design described throughout the manuscript.

claim: CUT&RUN allows for both quantitative high-resolution chromatin mapping and probing of the local chromatin environment.
source: Unlike Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP), which fragments and solubilizes total chromatin, CUT&RUN is performed in situ, allowing for both quantitative high-resolution chromatin mapping and probing of the local chromatin environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing high-resolution mapping and spike-in normalization for quantification.

claim: CUT&RUN yielded precise transcription factor profiles when applied to yeast and human nuclei while avoiding crosslinking and solubilization issues.
source: When applied to yeast and human nuclei, CUT&RUN yielded precise transcription factor profiles while avoiding crosslinking and solubilization issues.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from both yeast (Abf1, Reb1) and human (CTCF, Myc, Max) transcription factors presented in the results.

claim: CUT&RUN is simple to perform and is inherently robust.
source: CUT&RUN is simple to perform and is inherently robust, with extremely low backgrounds requiring only ~1/10th the sequencing depth as ChIP, making CUT&RUN especially cost-effective for transcription factor and chromatin profiling.
evidence: This is supported by the protocol description and comparison data showing consistent results across time points and conditions.

claim: CUT&RUN has extremely low backgrounds requiring only ~1/10th the sequencing depth as ChIP.
source: CUT&RUN is simple to perform and is inherently robust, with extremely low backgrounds requiring only ~1/10th the sequencing depth as ChIP, making CUT&RUN especially cost-effective for transcription factor and chromatin profiling.
evidence: This is supported by direct comparisons showing ~2-3 million reads for CUT&RUN versus ~20-30 million for ChIP-seq with comparable or better results.

claim: CUT&RUN mapped directional long range contact sites at high resolution when used in conjunction with native ChIP-seq and applied to human CTCF.
source: When used in conjunction with native ChIP-seq and applied to human CTCF, CUT&RUN mapped directional long range contact sites at high resolution.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of CUT&RUN and native ChIP data showing direct and indirect CTCF binding sites corresponding to ChIA-PET contact sites.

claim: ChIP is a protocol that has changed little since it was first introduced over 30 years ago.
source: TF profiling is most commonly carried out using chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), a protocol that has changed little since it was first introduced over 30 years ago (Solomon and Varshavsky, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original ChIP publication from 1985.

claim: Crosslinking can promote epitope masking and can generate false positive binding sites.
source: However, crosslinking can promote epitope masking and can generate false positive binding sites (Teytelman et al., 2013; Park et al., 2013; Jain et al., 2015; Baranello et al., 2016; Meyer and Liu, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies documenting these issues with crosslinking.

claim: Native ChIP provides a map of direct protein-DNA interactions with sensitivity and specificity trade-offs that compare favorably with X-ChIP methods.
source: 'Native' ChIP provides a map of direct protein-DNA interactions with sensitivity and specificity trade-offs that compare favorably with X-ChIP methods.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work and the comparative data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Native ChIP minimizes problems with epitope masking and improves efficiency relative to X-ChIP.
source: Native ChIP also minimizes problems with epitope masking and improves efficiency relative to X-ChIP, making it more amenable to low starting numbers of cells (O'Neill et al., 2006; Brind'Amour et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on native ChIP methods.

claim: Problems remain with native ChIP including incomplete extraction efficiency of protein-DNA complexes and the potential loss of binding.
source: But problems remain with incomplete extraction efficiency of protein-DNA complexes and the potential loss of binding.
evidence: This is based on known limitations of native ChIP methods discussed in the context of motivating the development of CUT&RUN.

claim: DamID resolution is limited by the distribution of GATC sites and cannot obtain the high resolution that is potentially attainable using a sequencing read-out.
source: However, as the resolution of DamID is limited by the distribution of GATC sites, DamID cannot obtain the high resolution that is potentially attainable using a sequencing read-out (Aughey and Southall, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation discussing the limitations of DamID resolution.

claim: ChEC-seq achieved near base-pair resolution.
source: We recently applied an Illumina sequencing read-out to ChEC (ChEC-seq), achieving near base-pair resolution (Zentner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work on ChEC-seq.

claim: Enzyme tethering methods fundamentally differ from ChIP because they are carried out in vivo (DamID) or in situ (ChEC), with extraction of DNA directly from live or permeabilized cells, thus eliminating the need to solubilize and recover chromatin.
source: Enzyme tethering methods fundamentally differ from ChIP because they are carried out in vivo (DamID) or in situ (ChEC), with extraction of DNA directly from live or permeabilized cells, thus eliminating the need to solubilize and recover chromatin.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction based on the methodological differences between enzyme tethering and ChIP approaches.

claim: Both DamID and ChEC require that a different chimeric fusion construct be produced for each TF to be mapped, limiting their transferability.
source: Both DamID and ChEC require that a different chimeric fusion construct be produced for each TF to be mapped, limiting their transferability, for example to animal models, patient biopsies and post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is based on the known requirements of these methods that necessitate genetic engineering for each target.

claim: Light MNase treatment of nuclei liberates mononucleosomes and TF-DNA complexes, leaving behind oligonucleosomes.
source: The CUT&RUN modifications of ChIC were motivated by the observation that light MNase treatment of nuclei liberates mononucleosomes and TF-DNA complexes, leaving behind oligonucleosomes (Sanders, 1978; Teves and Henikoff, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on MNase digestion of chromatin.

claim: Targeted cleavage on both sides of a TF releases the TF-DNA complex into the supernatant, leaving the remainder of the genome in the pelleted nuclei.
source: We expected that targeted cleavage on both sides of a TF would release the TF-DNA complex into the supernatant, leaving the remainder of the genome in the pelleted nuclei.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of CUT&RUN, supported by experimental data showing selective release of TF-bound fragments.

claim: Brief digestion reactions on ice recover TF-DNA complexes in the supernatant before TF-bound MNase diffuses around the genome and cleaves accessible chromatin.
source: By performing brief digestion reactions on ice, we would recover TF-DNA complexes in the supernatant before TF-bound MNase diffuses around the genome and cleaves accessible chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing low background and temperature-dependent specificity.

claim: Over a 100-fold digestion time course at 0°C, gradual cleavage and release of H2A fragments down to mononucleosomal size was observed, completely dependent on the presence of the primary antibody.
source: Indeed, over a 100-fold digestion time course at 0°C, we observed gradual cleavage and release of fragments down to mononucleosomal size, completely dependent on the presence of the primary antibody (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The size distributions of mapped fragments were virtually superimposable below ~150 bp for time points between 4 s and 128 s.
source: We found that the size distributions of mapped fragments were virtually superimposable below ~150 bp for time points between 4 s and 128 s (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the fragment size distribution data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The close concordance between time points over a 32-fold range suggests that limit digestion of TF-bound fragments occurs rapidly upon addition of Ca++.
source: This close concordance between time points over a 32-fold range suggests that limit digestion of TF-bound fragments occurs rapidly upon addition of Ca++, and demonstrates that digestion time is not a critical parameter.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing similar fragment size distributions across time points.

claim: Mapped TF fragment sizes peaked at ~100 bp, in contrast to H2A fragments, which peaked at ~150 bp.
source: Mapped TF fragment sizes peaked at ~100 bp, in contrast to H2A fragments, which peaked at ~150 bp.
evidence: This is supported by the fragment size distribution data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Total DNA extraction and purification of small fragments produced nearly identical results to supernatant extraction, demonstrating that extraction of DNA from the supernatant quantitatively recovers TF-bound fragments.
source: Total DNA extraction and purification of small fragments produced nearly identical results (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), which demonstrates that extraction of DNA from the supernatant quantitatively recovers TF-bound fragments.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Motifs based on CUT&RUN data and motifs based on ORGANIC data were nearly identical for Abf1 and Reb1.
source: To verify that the ≤120 bp fragments represent cleavages around TF binding sites, we first identified all significant Abf1 and Reb1 motifs in the genome and found that motifs based on CUT&RUN data and motifs based on ORGANIC data were nearly identical (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the motif comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The majority of peak calls overlapped the motif for each dataset, with somewhat better performance for CUT&RUN than ORGANIC for Abf1 and vice versa for Reb1.
source: We confirmed that the majority of peak calls overlapped the motif for each dataset, with somewhat better performance for CUT&RUN than ORGANIC for Abf1 and vice versa for Reb1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the peak-motif overlap analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4E.

claim: >90% of the TF sites were occupied by fragments over the corresponding motif relative to flanking regions for Abf1 and Reb1.
source: When rank-ordered by occupancy over the 2 kb interval centered over each Abf1 and Reb1 motif, we observed that >90% of the TF sites were occupied by fragments over the corresponding motif relative to flanking regions (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, upper panels), representing likely true positives.
evidence: This is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Abf1 fragments showed negligible occupancy at non-overlapping Reb1 sites and vice-versa for Reb1 fragments at non-overlapping Abf1 sites.
source: In contrast, Abf1 fragments showed negligible occupancy at non-overlapping Reb1 sites and vice-versa for Reb1 fragments at non-overlapping Abf1 sites (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, middle panels).
evidence: This is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 2 demonstrating specificity.

claim: The almost complete correspondence between the presence of a TF motif and occupancy of the TF, and the general absence at sites of a different TF, imply that CUT&RUN is both highly sensitive and specific for TF binding.
source: The almost complete correspondence between the presence of a TF motif and occupancy of the TF, and the general absence at sites of a different TF, imply that CUT&RUN is both highly sensitive and specific for TF binding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the motif occupancy and specificity data presented in Figure 2.

claim: CUT&RUN provides robust TF occupancy maps with improved sensitivity/specificity trade-offs relative to ChIP-seq.
source: Thus, CUT&RUN provides robust TF occupancy maps with improved sensitivity/specificity trade-offs relative to ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of CUT&RUN, ORGANIC, and standard ChIP-seq shown in Figure 2.

claim: CUT&RUN shows sharp 20 bp wide footprints for both Abf1 and Reb1, indicating that these transcription factors protect ~20 bp centered over the motif with near base-pair resolution.
source: For both Abf1 and Reb1, we observed sharp 20 bp wide footprints, indicating that these transcription factors protect ~20 bp centered over the motif with near base-pair resolution (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the footprint analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Upstream and downstream 'slopes' in the cleavage maps show a sawtooth pattern on either side of both Abf1 and Reb1 motifs, with distances between 'teeth' ~10 bp apart over >100 bp.
source: Interestingly, upstream and downstream 'slopes' in the cleavage maps show a sawtooth pattern on either side of both Abf1 and Reb1 motifs, with distances between 'teeth' ~10 bp apart over >100 bp, and confirmed by autocorrelation analysis to be independent of base composition (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the cleavage pattern and autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The 10 bp periodic cleavage preferences match the 10 bp/turn periodicity of B-form DNA, suggesting that the DNA on either side of these bound TFs is spatially oriented such that tethered MNase has preferential access to one face of the DNA double helix.
source: Such 10 bp periodic cleavage preferences match the 10 bp/turn periodicity of B-form DNA, which suggests that the DNA on either side of these bound TFs is spatially oriented such that tethered MNase has preferential access to one face of the DNA double helix.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed 10 bp periodicity and known DNA structure.

claim: Tethering of MNase to a TF constrains it to cleave nearby DNA even on the surface of a nucleosome, suggesting flexibility of the chromatin fiber.
source: Tethering of MNase to a TF constrains it to cleave nearby DNA even on the surface of a nucleosome, suggesting flexibility of the chromatin fiber (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed cleavage patterns extending beyond the immediate TF binding site.

claim: The very rapid kinetics observed at 0°C are due to immobilized MNase poised for cleavage near the tethering site.
source: Thus, the very rapid kinetics that we observe at 0°C are due to immobilized MNase poised for cleavage near the tethering site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid limit digestion observed in the time-course experiments.

claim: Mot1 CUT&RUN profiles are very similar to those obtained using ORGANIC profiling, but with only ~15% the number of paired-end reads.
source: When this modified protocol was applied to Mot1 over a >2 order-of-magnitude digestion range, we observed chromatin profiles that were very similar to those obtained using ORGANIC profiling, but with only ~15% the number of paired-end reads (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of Mot1 CUT&RUN and ORGANIC data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mot1 peaks on the upstream side of TBP binding sites, confirming that Mot1 approaches TBP from the upstream side in vivo as it does in vitro.
source: As expected, Mot1 peaks on the upstream side of TBP binding sites are seen for both CUT&RUN and ORGANIC profiles, confirming that Mot1 approaches TBP from the upstream side in vivo (Zentner and Henikoff, 2013) as it does in vitro (Wollmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the Mot1 profile data and citations to previous in vivo and in vitro studies.

claim: The ≤120 bp fragments track closely with TBP sites for Mot1, whereas the ≥150 bp fragments are diffusely distributed in the local vicinity, perhaps representing Mot1 translocation dynamics.
source: Heat map and average plot analyses show that the ≤120 bp fragments track closely with TBP sites, whereas the ≥150 bp fragments are diffusely distributed in the local vicinity, perhaps representing Mot1 translocation dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the heat map analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with speculation about the biological meaning.

claim: Sth1 peaks are most abundant in the NDRs, where CUT&RUN profiles show a gradual increase in yield with digestion times between 5 s and 10 min, indicating that quantitative limit digestions are obtained.
source: Sth1 peaks are most abundant in the NDRs, where CUT&RUN profiles show a gradual increase in yield with digestion times between 5 s and 10 min (Figure 4B), indicating that quantitative limit digestions are obtained using our protocol.
evidence: This is supported by the Sth1 time-course data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A nearly flat line was observed for the negative control derived from 3XFLAG-Sth1 nuclei treated in parallel for the maximum digestion time, but where the primary anti-FLAG antibody was omitted.
source: Importantly, we observed a nearly flat line for our negative control derived from 3XFLAG-Sth1 nuclei treated in parallel for the maximum digestion time, but where the primary anti-FLAG antibody was omitted.
evidence: This is supported by the negative control data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating specificity.

claim: Results for Sth1 CUT&RUN are similar to results for Sth1 ORGANIC profiling, but with much higher yield.
source: Our results for Sth1 CUT&RUN are similar to results for Sth1 ORGANIC profiling (Ramachandran et al., 2015), but with much higher yield (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of Sth1 CUT&RUN and ORGANIC data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CUT&RUN provides efficient high-resolution mapping of chromatin-associated complexes, even those that are very large and dynamic.
source: We conclude that CUT&RUN provides efficient high-resolution mapping of chromatin-associated complexes, even those that are very large and dynamic.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the successful mapping of Mot1 and Sth1, which are large dynamic complexes.

claim: There is only one centromeric nucleosome per chromosome in budding yeast, which is only ~1% the molar abundance of Abf1 or Reb1.
source: In budding yeast, there is only only one centromeric nucleosome per chromosome, which is only ~1% the molar abundance of Abf1 or Reb1.
evidence: This is based on known biology of yeast centromeres.

claim: The centromeric nucleosome contains the CenH3 (Cse4) histone variant in place of H3.
source: An additional challenge to studying the centromeric nucleosome, which contains the CenH3 (Cse4) histone variant in place of H3, is that it is part of the multi-megadalton kinetochore complex throughout the cell cycle (Akiyoshi et al., 2010), which renders it highly insoluble (Krassovsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on centromeric chromatin structure.

claim: The centromeric nucleosome is part of the multi-megadalton kinetochore complex throughout the cell cycle, which renders it highly insoluble.
source: An additional challenge to studying the centromeric nucleosome, which contains the CenH3 (Cse4) histone variant in place of H3, is that it is part of the multi-megadalton kinetochore complex throughout the cell cycle (Akiyoshi et al., 2010), which renders it highly insoluble (Krassovsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on kinetochore structure and solubility.

claim: The highest Cse4 occupancy on the chromosome is seen at the centromere for the insoluble kinetochore.
source: As expected for the insoluble kinetochore, the highest Cse4 occupancy on the chromosome is seen at the centromere (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the Cse4 occupancy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Occupancy of insoluble H2A, which is present in every nucleosome throughout the genome, is also maximum at the centromere.
source: Strikingly, occupancy of insoluble H2A, which is present in every nucleosome througout the genome, is also maximum at the centromere.
evidence: This is supported by the H2A occupancy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At all 16 yeast centromeres, very similar enrichments of Cse4 and H2A were observed confined to the ~120 bp functional centromere over the digestion time-course, with resolution that is 4-fold better than that of standard X-ChIP.
source: Indeed, at all 16 yeast centromeres we observe very similar enrichments of Cse4 and H2A confined to the ~120 bp functional centromere over the digestion time-course, with resolution that is 4-fold better than that of standard X-ChIP (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the centromere alignment data shown in Figure 5B and comparison to X-ChIP.

claim: Crosslinking results in a more distinct profile and the appearance of phased nucleosomes on either side of the centromere, which is interpreted as a reduction in chromatin flexibility with crosslinking.
source: Interestingly, crosslinking results in a more distinct profile and the appearance of phased nucleosomes on either side, which we interpret as a reduction in chromatin flexiblity with crosslinking, while demonstrating that the basic strategy can be applied to crosslinked cells.
evidence: This is supported by the crosslinked CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 5D, with interpretation of the biological meaning.

claim: The unequivocal presence of insoluble H2A in the centromeric nucleosome directly addresses the continuing controversy over its composition.
source: The unequivocal presence of insoluble H2A in the centromeric nucleosome directly addresses the continuing controversy over its composition (Wisniewski et al., 2014; Henikoff et al., 2014; Aravamudhan et al., 2013; Shivaraju et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the H2A data at centromeres and citations to publications debating centromere composition.

claim: The intactness of the centromeric particle over a >100 fold digestion time-course demonstrates that CUT&RUN is not biased by the inherent preference of MNase for AT-rich DNA.
source: Moreover, as the yeast centromeric nucleosome wraps DNA that is >90% A+T (Krassovsky et al., 2012), the intactness of the centromeric particle over a >100 fold digestion time-course (Figure 5) demonstrates that CUT&RUN is not biased by the inherent preference of MNase for AT-rich DNA (Chung et al., 2010; McGhee and Felsenfeld, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by the centromere data and citations regarding MNase sequence bias and centromere composition.

claim: CUT&RUN can map large DNA-binding complexes, even those that are rare, insoluble and AT-rich.
source: We conclude that CUT&RUN can map large DNA-binding complexes, even those that are rare, insoluble and AT-rich.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the successful mapping of the rare, insoluble, AT-rich centromeric nucleosome.

claim: Examination of the ≥150 bp profiles reveals broad peaks around the binding sites, sometimes with 'notches' corresponding to the sites themselves that deepen with time of digestion.
source: Examination of the ≥150 bp profiles (Figure 1D and Figure 4) reveals broad peaks around the binding sites, sometimes with 'notches' corresponding to the sites themselves that deepen with time of digestion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the ≥150 bp fragment profiles shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The broad peak pattern is interpreted as representing the gradual release of fragments with one end resulting from cleavage around the TF-DNA complex and a second cleavage that is close enough to the TF-bound site to produce a soluble fragment.
source: We interpret this pattern as representing the gradual release of fragments with one end resulting from cleavage around the TF-DNA complex and a second cleavage that is close enough to the TF-bound site to produce a soluble fragment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed ≥150 bp fragment patterns.

claim: Heat map analysis of the ≥150 bp fragments showed occupancy of Abf1 and Reb1 fragments over their respective binding motifs, extending ~0.5 kb on either side.
source: Heat map analysis of the ≥150 bp fragments also showed occupancy of Abf1 and Reb1 fragments over their respective binding motifs, extending ~0.5 kb on either side (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Extended local cleavage is reminiscent of the >1 kb reach of DamID, suggesting that the flexibility of the tether results in probing of nearby chromatin.
source: Such extended local cleavage is reminiscent of the >1 kb reach of DamID (van Steensel et al., 2001), which suggests that the flexibility of the tether results in probing of nearby chromatin.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to DamID and the observed extended cleavage patterns.

claim: CTCF CUT&RUN showed higher dynamic range than other profiling methods, including standard X-ChIP-seq and ChIP-exo, when comparing 10 million randomly selected reads.
source: To directly compare the efficiency of various methods, we randomly selected 10 million reads for each technique and plotted the raw scores as an indication of information content per sequenced read. As was the case for yeast TFs, CTCF CUT&RUN showed higher dynamic range than other profiling methods, including standard X-ChIP-seq and ChIP-exo (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of CTCF profiling methods shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When aligned to CTCF motifs found within DNaseI hypersensitive sites or previously identified binding sites, CUT&RUN and X-ChIP-seq CTCF heat maps showed strong concordance, with CUT&RUN having a higher dynamic range.
source: When aligned to CTCF motifs found within DNaseI hypersensitive sites or previously identified binding sites, CUT&RUN and X-ChIP-seq CTCF heat maps showed strong concordance, with CUT&RUN having a higher dynamic range (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the heat map comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A no antibody control showed undetectable background when CUT&RUN is performed at low temperature.
source: A no antibody control showed undetectable background (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) when CUT&RUN is performed at low temperature (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the negative control data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: CUT&RUN releases neighboring fragments corresponding to phased nucleosomes immediately adjacent to CTCF sites.
source: As was the case for budding yeast TFs, we observed release of the neighboring fragments, which correspond to phased nucleosomes immediately adjacent to CTCF sites.
evidence: This is supported by the ≥150 bp fragment data showing nucleosome-sized fragments flanking CTCF sites.

claim: Pronounced 'tram-tracks' separated by 44 bp at defined positions relative to the CTCF motif were observed by plotting just the end positions of the short CUT&RUN fragments.
source: By plotting just the end positions of the short CUT&RUN fragments that are the cleavage positions of the tethered MNase, we observed pronounced 'tram-tracks' separated by 44 bp at defined positions relative to the CTCF motif.
evidence: This is supported by the fragment end position analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The exact cleavage pattern is consistent over a ~300 fold time-course digestion range, with a predominant single base-pair cut site on either side of the CTCF-bound site, highlighting the limit digest obtained.
source: Furthermore, the exact cleavage pattern is consistent over a ~300 fold time-course digestion range, with a predominant single base-pair cut site on either side of the CTCF-bound site, highlighting the limit digest obtained (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the time-course cleavage pattern data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The cleavage pattern indicates that the cleavage positions are precise and highly homogeneous within the population of cells.
source: This pattern indicates that the cleavage positions are precise and highly homogeneous within the population of cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistent cleavage patterns observed across the cell population.

claim: CUT&RUN accurately maps both the TFs and their flanking chromatin in the same experiment.
source: Our results suggest that CUT&RUN accurately maps both the TFs and their flanking chromatin in the same experiment.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of both TF footprints and flanking nucleosomes in the same dataset.

claim: CUT&RUN successfully mapped both Myc and Max at high resolution.
source: We therefore tested CUT&RUN using Myc and Max which are basic-loop-helix proteins that bind to a short E-box motif and have b residence times (Phair et al., 2004). CUT&RUN successfully mapped both Myc and Max at high resolution (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the Myc and Max mapping data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: For Max, CUT&RUN had a much higher dynamic range than ENCODE ChIP-seq and was able to robustly identify a much larger number of Max binding sites.
source: In the case of Max, a quantitative comparison with ENCODE ChIP-seq data is possible as the same antibody was used, and here CUT&RUN had a much higher dynamic range and therefore was able to robustly identify a much larger number of Max binding sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of Max CUT&RUN and ENCODE ChIP-seq shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Max is present at almost all Myc binding sites, as expected since Myc forms a heterodimer with Max to bind DNA at E-boxes.
source: To bind DNA at E-boxes, Myc forms a heterodimer with Max (Blackwood et al., 1991) but in addition Max has other binding partners (Ayer and Eisenman, 1993), As expected, we see very high overlap with Max present at almost all Myc binding sites.
evidence: This is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and citations to studies on Myc-Max heterodimerization.

claim: There is poor overlap between previously identified binding sites by ENCODE X-ChIP-seq for Myc and Max, as 10-fold fewer Max sites were identified.
source: In contrast, there is poor overlap between previously identified binding sites by ENCODE X-ChIP-seq for Myc and Max, as 10-fold fewer Max sites were identified.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of ENCODE peak calls shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: When Max ENCODE X-ChIP-seq data were lined up over Max CUT&RUN sites, high occupancy was observed, suggesting that the lower dynamic range of X-ChIP-seq relative to CUT&RUN was responsible for the failure to identify these Max binding sites by X-ChIP-seq.
source: However, when we lined up Max ENCODE X-ChIP-seq data over Max CUT&RUN sites, we saw high occupancy (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that the lower dynamic range of X-ChIP-seq relative to CUT&RUN was responsible for the failure to identify these Max binding sites by X-ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: By analyzing 10 million reads from CUT&RUN and ENCODE X-ChIP-seq, similar H3K27me3 landscapes were observed, but at a much higher dynamic range for CUT&RUN.
source: By analyzing 10 million reads from CUT&RUN and ENCODE X-ChIP-seq, we observed similar H3K27me3 landscapes, but at a much higher dynamic range for CUT&RUN, which demonstrates that Protein A-MNase is able to access compacted chromatin (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the H3K27me3 comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Protein A-MNase is able to access compacted chromatin.
source: By analyzing 10 million reads from CUT&RUN and ENCODE X-ChIP-seq, we observed similar H3K27me3 landscapes, but at a much higher dynamic range for CUT&RUN, which demonstrates that Protein A-MNase is able to access compacted chromatin (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the successful mapping of H3K27me3, a mark associated with compacted heterochromatin.

claim: H3K27me3 cleaved chromatin is readily released from the intact nuclei into the soluble fraction, indicating that CUT&RUN is applicable to probing protein-DNA interactions in compacted chromatin.
source: Furthermore, H3K27me3 cleaved chromatin is readily released from the intact nuclei into the soluble fraction, indicating that CUT&RUN is applicable to probing protein-DNA interactions in compacted chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by the H3K27me3 data showing release of fragments into the soluble fraction.

claim: Native ChIP mapping of CTCF identified 2298 sites with high motif scores.
source: We developed a new native ChIP protocol (Appendix 1), and achieved near-complete protein extraction with no evidence of protein redistribution (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). Under native conditions, we identified 2298 sites with high motif scores.
evidence: This is supported by the native ChIP data and peak calling results.

claim: CUT&RUN mapping of CTCF detected ~22,000 sites that were also present in X-ChIP, with a diverse range of motif scores.
source: In contrast, CUT&RUN mapping of CTCF detected ~22,000 sites that were also present in X-ChIP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), with a diverse range of motif scores (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the CUT&RUN peak calling and motif score analysis.

claim: All sites identified by native ChIP were robustly detected by CUT&RUN and X-ChIP, showing a similar signal distribution.
source: As expected, all sites identified by native ChIP also were robustly detected by CUT&RUN and X-ChIP, showing a similar signal distribution (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CUT&RUN sites lacking a significant native ChIP signal nevertheless showed a robust footprint in the native ChIP input with a similar cumulative distribution of counts, indicating the presence of unknown bound factors.
source: CUT&RUN sites lacking a significant native ChIP signal nevertheless showed a robust footprint in the native ChIP input with a similar cumulative distribution of counts (Figure 7B), indicating the presence of unknown bound factors, as would be expected for 3D genomic interactions.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7B, with inference about 3D interactions.

claim: CUT&RUN, as with X-ChIP, can discover both direct (native CTCF peak) and indirect (CUT&RUN peak only) chromatin interactions at high resolution.
source: This suggests that CUT&RUN, as with X-ChIP, can discover both direct (native CTCF peak) and indirect (CUT&RUN peak only) chromatin interactions at high resolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of native ChIP and CUT&RUN peak calls.

claim: For a typical ~1 Mb genomic region, all high-scoring ChIA-PET fragments overlap with direct and indirect sites.
source: We find that for a typical ~1 Mb genomic region all high-scoring ChIA-PET fragments overlap with direct and indirect sites (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by the ChIA-PET overlap analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: 91% of the direct sites are present in CTCF ChIA-PET data, with 43% of these ChIA-PET fragments interacting with an indirect site.
source: Moreover, 91% of the direct sites are present in CTCF ChIA-PET data, with 43% of these ChIA-PET fragments interacting with an indirect site, and the remainder contained a high CUT&RUN signal (Figure 8C), which suggests these are indirect sites involved in multiple contacts, just below the peak calling threshold.
evidence: This is supported by the ChIA-PET interaction analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: A high frequency of Hi-C interactions between direct sites and indirect sites was found, with a quantitative correlation between Hi-C score and CUT&RUN signal at the indirect sites.
source: As further evidence that CUT&RUN can detect indirect contact interactions, we found a high frequency of Hi-C interactions between direct sites and indirect sites and a quantitative correlation between Hi-C score and CUT&RUN signal at the indirect sites (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the Hi-C correlation analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: By comparing CUT&RUN and native ChIP it is possible to map contact sites at near base-pair resolution, to distinguish direct from indirect protein binding sites that result from long-range genomic interactions, and to determine the directionality to these contacts.
source: Therefore, by comparing CUT&RUN and native ChIP it is possible to map contact sites at near base-pair resolution, to distinguish direct from indirect protein binding sites that result from long-range genomic interactions, and to determine the directionality to these contacts, not feasible by other methods.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined analysis of CUT&RUN, native ChIP, ChIA-PET, and Hi-C data.

claim: When normalized to spike-in DNA, the number of cleavage events is proportional to the starting cell number.
source: When normalized to spike-in DNA, we observed that the number of cleavage events is proportional to the starting cell number (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by the cell titration experiment shown in Figure 9.

claim: When the data are normalized to the total number of reads aligning to the human genome, there is no clear difference in the samples, suggesting that high data quality is maintained with low input material.
source: Furthermore, when the data are normalized to the total number of reads aligning to the human genome, there is no clear difference in the samples, suggesting that high data quality is maintained with low input material.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of standard normalization across different cell numbers shown in Figure 9.

claim: CUT&RUN performs as well as or better than ChIP-seq with respect to simplicity, resolution, robustness, efficiency, data quality, and applicability to highly insoluble complexes.
source: We find that CUT&RUN performs as well as or better than ChIP-seq with respect to simplicity, resolution, robustness, efficiency, data quality, and applicability to highly insoluble complexes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the comparative data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CUT&RUN requires only ~1/10th of the sequencing depth of other high resolution methodologies due to the intrinsically low background achieved by performing the reaction in situ.
source: CUT&RUN requires only ~1/10th of the sequencing depth of other high resolution methodologies due to the intrinsically low background achieved by performing the reaction in situ.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative sequencing depth requirements shown throughout the results.

claim: CUT&RUN can probe the local environment around the targeted site because nuclei are intact when MNase is activated.
source: As nuclei are intact when MNase is activated, CUT&RUN can probe the local environment around the targeted site.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of flanking nucleosomes and extended cleavage patterns.

claim: CUT&RUN recovers sites of 3D contacts with base-pair resolution at relatively low sequencing depth in human cells.
source: Indeed, we find that CUT&RUN recovers sites of 3D contacts with base-pair resolution at relatively low sequencing depth in human cells.
evidence: This is supported by the CTCF contact site mapping data.

claim: CUT&RUN is antibody-based, so that it can be applied to any epitope on chromatin, making it a general method for chromatin profiling.
source: Like ChIP, CUT&RUN is antibody-based, so that it can be applied to any epitope on chromatin, making it a general method for chromatin profiling that takes advantage of the large antibody production infrastructure developed for ChIP.
evidence: This is based on the antibody-based design of CUT&RUN and the demonstration with multiple different targets.

claim: CUT&RUN provides quantitative occupancy profiles with standard and spike-in normalization options.
source: CUT&RUN provides quantitative occupancy profiles with standard and spike-in normalization options implemented by our custom software for processing and comparing ChIP-seq and CUT&RUN datasets.
evidence: This is supported by the normalization methods described and demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: The only non-standard feature of CUT&RUN is the requirement for the pA-MN fusion protein, which can be produced and purified in a batch from bacterial culture that yields enough pA-MN for profiling >100,000 samples.
source: The only non-standard feature of CUT&RUN is the requirement for the pA-MN fusion protein, which can be produced and purified in a batch from bacterial culture that yields enough pA-MN for profiling >100,000 samples.
evidence: This is based on the protocol for pA-MN production and the amounts required per reaction.

claim: CUT&RUN can resolve crosslinking-, sonication- and solubilization-related issues because it is based on different principles from ChIP.
source: As CUT&RUN is based on different principles from ChIP, it can resolve crosslinking-, sonication- and solubilization-related issues.
evidence: This is based on the in situ nature of CUT&RUN and the absence of these steps in the protocol.

claim: Backgrounds are low with CUT&RUN because cleavages occur only around binding sites, whereas ChIP first pulverizes the entire genome.
source: Backgrounds are low with CUT&RUN, because cleavages occur only around binding sites, whereas ChIP first pulverizes the entire genome, and these fragments contribute to a genome-wide background noise that must still be sequenced.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the observed low background in CUT&RUN.

claim: The near absence of detectable background under brief low-temperature conditions, the lack of preference for accessible or AT-rich DNA, and the recovery of essentially all Abf1 and Reb1 motifs in the yeast genome suggest that CUT&RUN is not subject to the types of artifacts that sometimes have plagued ChIP.
source: The near absence of detectable background under the brief low-temperature conditions that we used, the lack of preference for accessible or AT-rich DNA, and the recovery of essentially all Abf1 and Reb1 motifs in the yeast genome, suggests that CUT&RUN is not subject to the types of artifacts that sometimes have plagued ChIP (Teytelman et al., 2013; Park et al., 2013; Jain et al., 2015; Baranello et al., 2016; Kasinathan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to studies documenting ChIP artifacts.

claim: CUT&RUN antibody binding takes place in an intact nuclear environment resembling conditions for immunofluorescence microscopy, so that it should be successful for antibodies that are validated cytologically, even those that fail in ChIP.
source: Furthermore, CUT&RUN antibody binding takes place in an intact nuclear environment resembling conditions for immunofluorescence microscopy, so that it should be successful for antibodies that are validated cytologically, even those that fail in ChIP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in situ nature of antibody binding in CUT&RUN.

claim: CUT&RUN should be appropriate for extending classical chromatin salt-fractionation to specific TFs and chromatin complexes because it solubilizes chromatin only after the targeted cleavage reaction.
source: As CUT&RUN solubilizes chromatin only after the targeted cleavage reaction, it should be appropriate for extending classical chromatin salt-fractionation (Sanders, 1978; Teves and Henikoff, 2012; Jahan et al., 2016) to specific TFs and chromatin complexes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the compatibility of CUT&RUN with differential solubility, supported by the centromere data.

claim: The long reach of antibody-tethered MNase can probe the local environment in intact nuclei.
source: A consequence of using intact nuclei for CUT&RUN is that the long reach of antibody-tethered MNase can probe the local environment.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of extended cleavage patterns and flanking nucleosomes.

claim: In yeast, cleavages on one surface of the DNA flanking the TF were observed, gradually decreasing with distance.
source: In yeast, we observed cleavages on one surface of the DNA flanking the TF, gradually decreasing with distance.
evidence: This is supported by the 10 bp periodic cleavage pattern observed in Figure 3.

claim: In human cells, cleavages at sites previously identified as contact sites for CTCF were observed.
source: In human cells, we observed cleavages at sites previously identified as contact sites for CTCF.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison with ChIA-PET and Hi-C data.

claim: Hi-C contact sites have been predicted computationally with a high degree of confidence given sites of CTCF binding.
source: Recently, Hi-C contact sites have been predicted computationally with a high degree of confidence given sites of CTCF binding (Sanborn et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published computational study.

claim: CUT&RUN can provide a complete high-resolution 1D map of a genome while enriching its 3D contact map with high-resolution distinctions between direct and indirect TF binding sites.
source: As CUT&RUN maps both CTCF binding sites and interactions, and our native ChIP protocol identifies those sites that are directly TF-bound, it can provide a complete high-resolution 1D map of a genome while enriching its 3D contact map with high-resolution distinctions between direct and indirect TF binding sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined CUT&RUN and native ChIP data for CTCF.

claim: ChIP-seq analysis typically includes normalization to compensate for different numbers of reads between samples.
source: ChIP-seq analysis typically includes normalization to compensate for different numbers of reads between samples.
evidence: This is based on standard practices in ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: In ChIP-seq, whole genome fragmentation leads to a constant low density genome-wide background that provides a basis for normalization.
source: In ChIP-seq, whole genome fragmentation leads to a constant low density genome-wide background that provides a basis for normalization, for example, in comparing wildtype and knockdown cell lines.
evidence: This is based on the principles of ChIP-seq normalization.

claim: Normalization fails on abundant proteins in ChIP-seq, but this can be corrected by the use of spike-in controls.
source: Although normalization fails on abundant proteins, this can be corrected by the use of spike-in controls (Bonhoure et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015; Orlando et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on spike-in normalization for ChIP-seq.

claim: A rigorous spike-in strategy for ChIP-seq requires the addition of cells from a different species, and quantification is reliant upon antibody cross-reactivity.
source: However, a rigorous spike-in strategy requires the addition of cells from a different species, and quantification is reliant upon antibody cross-reactivity (Orlando et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing spike-in methods for ChIP-seq.

claim: Simply adding a constant low amount of fragmented spike-in DNA from a different species suffices for CUT&RUN normalization and allows accurate quantification of protein occupancy.
source: To normalize between samples despite the low background in CUT&RUN, we find that simply adding a constant low amount of fragmented spike-in DNA from a different species suffices and allows accurate quantification of protein occupancy.
evidence: This is supported by the spike-in normalization experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Only ~10 million paired-end reads were required for each CTCF time point, similar to the requirement for low-resolution ChIP-seq, and many fewer than for ChIP-exo, which required ~100 million reads for CTCF.
source: For example only ~10 million paired-end reads were required for each CTCF time point, similar to the requirement for low-resolution ChIP-seq, and many fewer than for ChIP-exo, which required ~100 million reads for CTCF (Rhee and Pugh, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing depth comparisons and citation to ChIP-exo requirements.

claim: In the cases of Max and H3K27me3, 10 million reads for CUT&RUN provided very high dynamic range, but 10 million reads were insufficient for calling peaks from Max ENCODE X-ChIP-seq.
source: Furthermore, in the cases of Max and H3K27me3, 10 million reads for CUT&RUN provided very high dynamic range, but 10 million reads were insufficient for calling peaks from Max ENCODE X-ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of Max and H3K27me3 data.

claim: The cost-effectiveness of CUT&RUN makes it attractive as a replacement for ChIP-seq especially where depth of sequencing is limiting.
source: This cost-effectiveness makes CUT&RUN attractive as a replacement for ChIP-seq especially where depth of sequencing is limiting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lower sequencing requirements of CUT&RUN.

claim: The high efficiency of CUT&RUN can be attributed to fundamental differences between in situ profiling and ChIP: CUT&RUN retains the in vivo 3D conformation, so antibodies access only exposed surfaces in a first-order binding reaction, whereas in ChIP, antibodies interact with the solubilizable genome-wide content of the pulverized cells or nuclei.
source: We might attribute the high efficiency of CUT&RUN to fundamental differences between in situ profiling and ChIP: CUT&RUN retains the in vivo 3D conformation, so antibodies access only exposed surfaces in a first-order binding reaction, whereas in ChIP, antibodies interact with the solubilizable genome-wide content of the pulverized cells or nuclei.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the observed efficiency differences.

claim: CUT&RUN cleavage is effectively a zero-order reaction, resulting in steady particle release during the brief low temperature time-course for all bound epitopes in the genome.
source: Furthermore, CUT&RUN cleavage is effectively a zero-order reaction, resulting in steady particle release during the brief low temperature time-course for all bound epitopes in the genome.
evidence: This is supported by the consistent cleavage patterns across time points.

claim: Mapping of ~22,000 direct and indirect CTCF sites with 600,000 cells is comparable to the sensitivity of ultra-low input ChIP-seq protocols that are typically restricted to abundant histone modifications, such as H3K27me3, with ~5000 cells.
source: Accounting for epitope abundances, we estimate that our mapping of ~22,000 direct and indirect CTCF sites with 600,000 cells is comparable to the sensitivity of ultra-low input ChIP-seq protocols that are typically restricted to abundant histone modifications, such as H3K27me3, with ~5000 cells (Brind'Amour et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the cell number requirements and citation to ultra-low input ChIP methods.

claim: Ultra-low-input ChIP provides only ~2 kb resolution, whereas CUT&RUN provides near base-pair resolution.
source: Whereas ultra-low-input ChIP provides only ~2 kb resolution, CUT&RUN provides near base-pair resolution.
evidence: This is based on the known resolution limitations of ultra-low input ChIP and the demonstrated high resolution of CUT&RUN.

claim: The inherent robustness, high information content, low input and sequencing requirements and suitability for automation of CUT&RUN suggest that it might be applied to epigenome diagnostics.
source: The inherent robustness, high information content, low input and sequencing requirements and suitability for automation of our method suggests that CUT&RUN profiling of CTCF and other TFs might be applied to epigenome diagnostics.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications based on the demonstrated properties of CUT&RUN.

claim: In situ mapping of protein-DNA interactions by CUT&RUN is an attractive alternative to ChIP-seq.
source: We conclude that in situ mapping of protein-DNA interactions by CUT&RUN is an attractive alternative to ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by all the comparative data presented.

claim: CUT&RUN has a number of practical advantages over ChIP and its derivatives: low background resulting in low sequence depth requirements, ease of use making it amenable to robotic automation, and allowing accurate quantification with a simple spike-in strategy.
source: In summary, CUT&RUN has a number of practical advantages over ChIP and its derivatives: with low background resulting in low sequence depth requirements, the ease of use makes it amenable to robotic automation, while allowing accurate quantification with a simple spike-in strategy.
evidence: This is a summary of the practical advantages demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: Abf1 has two DNA-binding domains spaced ~10 bp apart.
source: Abf1 has two DNA-binding domains spaced ~10 bp apart (Cho et al., 1995), whereas Reb1 has a single Myb-like DNA-binding domain (Morrow et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published structural studies.

claim: Reb1 has a single Myb-like DNA-binding domain.
source: Abf1 has two DNA-binding domains spaced ~10 bp apart (Cho et al., 1995), whereas Reb1 has a single Myb-like DNA-binding domain (Morrow et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published structural study.
